newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Bhutto party wants peace with Pakistan ethnic MQM.
newsitem.headline: Bhutto party wants peace with Pakistan ethnic MQM.

text.p: Ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party (PPP) said on Saturday it wanted to end hostility with the ethnic Mohajir National Movement (MQM) in the southern province of Sindh.

"We extend our hands for friendship with the MQM and all the rest of the forces for restoration of peace and stability in Sindh," said Amin Fahim, a PPP figure asked by his party to try to form the provincial government.

"There has been enough of uncertainty, anarchy and bitterness," he told a news conference in Karachi, provincial capital and Pakistan's commercial hub, which has been hit by years of ethnic and political violence for which the MQM has been blamed most.

The PPP, routed by former prime minister Nawaz Sharif's Pakistan Muslim League (PML) party in Monday's general election, has named Fahim to contest for the chief ministership of Sindh, Bhutto's home province, where it remained the largest party with 36 seats.
But the PPP is far short of a simple majority, which it had in the previous house with 56 seats won in the 1993 elections.
The MQM has won 28 seats and the Pakistan Muslim League (PML) 14 seats in the 109-seat house.
"There should be a government of consensus in Sindh," Fahim said. "I have a mandate from my party to minimise political differences and bring peace."

The MQM, which speaks for Urdu-speaking people who migrated from India at Partition in 1947 and their descendants, has been accusing Bhutto's government of excesses and extrajudicial killings in Karachi during its crackdown on violence.
The PPP blamed the MQM for much of the violence and in Karachi in which over 2,500 people died since 1995.
Fahim said that being the largest party in Sindh, the PPP had the democratic right to be the first to be called by the provincial governor to form the government.
The PML says it will also contact the MQM, independents and other smaller parties to form the government in Sindh. But party sources said it was premature to give details of the approaches.
Political analysts say government-formation in Sindh, which has a history of bloody political unrest and ethnic polarisation, will be a tricky affair.
